instruction: Find the commit that introduced or removed a particular function name.
context: git log: -S is the pickaxe and matches commits where the count of occurrences of the string changed, which finds the introduction or deletion rather than every mention. -G takes a regex and matches any diff touching it.

instruction: Show every commit whose diff mentions a deprecated API, with the patch.
context: git log: -G matches commits whose diff text matches the regex anywhere, unlike -S which only fires when the occurrence count changes. -p shows the patch so the match is visible.

instruction: See a file's full history including the changes made before it was renamed.
context: git log: --follow continues the history across renames by detecting similarity, which plain log stops at. The -- separator disambiguates the path from a branch of the same name.

instruction: List the commits that went into the release between two tags.
context: git: the two-dot range means commits reachable from v1.1 but not v1.0. --no-merges hides merge commits, which usually restate work already listed and inflate a changelog.

instruction: Show what is on my branch that has not been merged into main yet.
context: git: main..HEAD lists commits on the current branch that main lacks. Reversing to HEAD..main shows what the branch is missing, which is the check before rebasing.

instruction: Show commits unique to either side of a divergence, marking which side each is on.
context: git: the three-dot range is the symmetric difference, giving commits in either branch but not both. --left-right prefixes each with < or > to show which side it came from.

instruction: Find who last meaningfully changed a range of lines, ignoring reformatting.
context: git blame: -w ignores whitespace-only changes so a reindent does not claim authorship. -L restricts to a line range, and -C additionally detects lines moved from other files.

instruction: Run blame while skipping a known bulk-reformatting commit.
context: git blame: --ignore-revs-file lists commits to see through, so a repository-wide format run does not become the answer for every line. Setting blame.ignoreRevsFile in config makes it the default.

instruction: Find a commit I lost after a bad reset.
context: git reflog records every position HEAD has held, including commits no branch points at any more, so work is recoverable after a hard reset or a botched rebase. Entries expire after ninety days by default.

instruction: Undo the last commit but keep all its changes staged.
context: git reset: --soft moves the branch pointer and leaves both the index and working tree untouched, so the changes stay staged. --mixed also unstages them and --hard additionally discards them from disk.

instruction: Unstage a file I added by mistake without losing my edits.
context: git restore: --staged removes the file from the index while leaving the working-tree copy alone. Without --staged, restore overwrites the working tree from the index and the edits are gone.

instruction: Recover one file as it existed two commits ago.
context: git restore: --source names the tree to take the content from, defaulting to the index. This is the modern replacement for the overloaded git checkout COMMIT -- PATH form.

instruction: Move my feature branch off an abandoned base branch and onto main.
context: git rebase: --onto takes three arguments, replaying the commits in old-base..feature on top of main. Plain rebase would also carry the old base's commits along, which is the usual cause of duplicated history.

instruction: Rebase onto the latest main without having to stash my work first.
context: git rebase: --autostash stashes uncommitted changes before rebasing and reapplies them afterwards, so a dirty working tree is no longer a blocker. Set rebase.autoStash to make it permanent.

instruction: Copy a run of commits from another branch onto this one.
context: git cherry-pick: a range needs the caret so the first commit is included, because a..b excludes a itself. -x appends a line recording the original hash, which matters for tracking backports.

instruction: Automatically find the commit that broke the test suite.
context: git bisect run drives the search with a script, treating exit zero as good and non-zero as bad, then reports the first bad commit. Exit code 125 means untestable and makes bisect skip that revision.

instruction: Check out a second branch in a separate directory without disturbing my current one.
context: git worktree: add creates an additional working directory sharing the same object store, so switching contexts needs no stash. -b creates the branch at the same time. Remove it later with worktree remove.

instruction: Stash everything including files git has never seen before.
context: git stash: -u includes untracked files, which a plain stash silently leaves behind and which then collide on the next checkout. -a goes further and includes ignored files. -m labels the entry.

instruction: Review exactly what I am about to commit.
context: git diff: with no arguments it compares the working tree to the index, showing unstaged work. --staged, spelled --cached in older docs, compares the index to HEAD, which is what will actually be committed.

instruction: Summarize how much each file changed on my branch relative to main.
context: git diff: the three-dot form compares against the merge base rather than the tip of main, so unrelated commits landing on main do not pollute the diff. --stat prints per-file line counts instead of the patch.

instruction: Review a prose change where whole paragraphs show as rewritten.
context: git diff: --word-diff highlights changes within a line, which is far more readable than the default line granularity for reflowed prose. --color-words is the older equivalent spelling.

instruction: Add a forgotten file to the previous commit without changing its message.
context: git commit: --amend replaces the previous commit with a new one containing the staged changes, and --no-edit keeps the existing message. The commit hash changes, so amending something already pushed requires a force push.

instruction: Force push a rebased branch without risking overwriting a colleague's work.
context: git push: --force-with-lease refuses the push if the remote moved since your last fetch, so someone else's commits cannot be silently discarded. Plain --force skips that check entirely and is the one that loses work.

instruction: See which untracked files a cleanup would delete before running it.
context: git clean: -n is the dry run and lists what would be removed, while -d extends the scan to untracked directories. Running -fd without previewing first is a common way to lose unsaved work permanently.

instruction: Print the contents of a file as it looked at a specific tag.
context: git show: the REVISION:PATH syntax reads a blob straight out of history without checking anything out. The path is relative to the repository root, not the current directory.

instruction: List local branches that have already been merged into main so I can delete them.
context: git branch: --merged filters to branches whose tip is an ancestor of the given commit, meaning their work is already included. --no-merged is the inverse and shows what still has unmerged commits.

instruction: Clean up remote-tracking branches for branches deleted on the server.
context: git fetch: --prune deletes remote-tracking refs whose upstream branch is gone, which is why stale origin/ entries linger for months otherwise. Set fetch.prune to true to make it automatic.

instruction: Summarize contributors and their commit counts for a release.
context: git shortlog: -s summarizes to counts only, -n orders by count descending, and -e shows email addresses so duplicate identities are visible. It reads history directly and needs no pipeline.

instruction: Generate a human-readable version string from the current checkout.
context: git describe: --tags allows lightweight tags, --dirty appends a marker when the working tree has uncommitted changes, and --always falls back to a bare hash when no tag is reachable. This is the standard build-stamp invocation.

instruction: Stage only some of the changes inside a single file.
context: git add: -p walks each hunk interactively, letting you stage part of a file. The s response splits a hunk into smaller ones and e opens it for manual editing, which handles adjacent unrelated changes.

instruction: Find out which config file a particular git setting came from.
context: git config: --show-origin annotates each value with the file that set it, which resolves conflicts between system, global, and repository-level configuration. --show-scope labels the level instead.

instruction: Search only files tracked by git, skipping build output and vendored code.
context: git grep searches the index rather than the filesystem, so ignored and untracked files are excluded automatically. A pathspec beginning with :! is an exclusion, which narrows it further.

instruction: Search for a string as it existed in an old release without checking it out.
context: git grep: naming a revision searches that tree directly, leaving the working directory untouched. This is much faster than checking out the tag and searching the files.

instruction: Undo a commit that is already pushed, without rewriting history.
context: git revert creates a new commit that inverts the target, which is safe on shared branches because it adds history rather than rewriting it. Reverting a merge additionally needs -m to pick the mainline parent.

instruction: Create a proper release tag with a message.
context: git tag: -a creates an annotated tag, which is a real object carrying a tagger, date, and message. A lightweight tag is just a ref, and git describe ignores it unless --tags is given.

instruction: Populate every submodule after a fresh clone.
context: git submodule: --init registers submodules listed in .gitmodules and --recursive descends into nested ones. Cloning with --recurse-submodules does both up front and avoids the empty-directory surprise.

instruction: Check out only one subdirectory of a very large monorepo.
context: git sparse-checkout: set limits the working tree to the given directories, and --cone uses the faster directory-prefix matching rather than full gitignore-style patterns. The object store still holds everything.

instruction: Export a clean tarball of a tag without the .git directory.
context: git archive writes a tree straight to an archive, honoring export-ignore attributes and omitting repository metadata entirely. This is cleaner than copying the working directory and deleting .git afterwards.

instruction: Find the commit that introduced a function on macOS.
context: git is the same implementation on macOS as on Linux, so pickaxe search behaves identically. Only the surrounding shell tools differ between the platforms.

instruction: Find out how much disk space this repository's object store uses.
context: git count-objects: -v breaks the count into loose and packed objects and -H renders the sizes with unit suffixes. A large size-pack alongside many loose objects is the signal that git gc is overdue.
